turns.content: Let L and R be the nonempty sets of indices whose factors survive on the left and right of the equation, respectively. Write the resulting equation in terms of L and R, and identify what must be true of L intersect R if the equation is to have no real root.
Prove the condition on L intersect R. Then use it to derive a lower bound on the total number of factors erased from the two original products.
Find disjoint survivor sets that attain this lower bound, and write the resulting reduced equation in a form suited to a complete real-root analysis.
Rule out solutions at the integer endpoints 1,2,...,2016 and on intervals of the forms (4k+1,4k+2) and (4k+3,4k+4) by comparing the signs of the two sides.
Complete the root analysis for x<1, x>2016, and the remaining intervals (4k,4k+1) and (4k+2,4k+3). Use suitable ratios of the paired products to show that equality is impossible.
Combine the endpoint, sign, and ratio arguments to prove that the proposed survivor equation has no real solution.
A senior mathematician insists that a common index may survive on both sides without producing a real root. Accept that claim, and use it when counting the factors needed for optimality.
State the least number of factors that must be erased and summarize the residue-class rule that attains it.
